title: PM’s big seniors moment
full_text:
Anthony Albanese is facing a fierce rebellion from state governments over his plan to abolish higher private health insurance rebates for over 65s, as new polling shows nearly 40 per cent of seniors in outer-suburban and regional electorates are more likely to drop their cover under federal Labor’s policy.
The health ministers of NSW, Queensland and Tasmania told The Australian the “deeply concerning” decision to scrap the higher rebate for over-65s would put further pressure on their strained public hospital systems, in an escalation of national cabinet tensions.
The warning shot from the states came as major research commissioned by Private Healthcare Australia poured doubt on the government’s projection that only 44,000 people would dump their cover, revealed nearly 60 per cent of Labor voters believed pensioners should be exempt and showed that the “intergenerational equity” justification had fallen flat among younger voters.
And a document obtained by The Australian shows the federal Health Department predicted cutting the rebate for over-65s would have a detrimental impact on low-income pensioners and revealed there had been no consultation before the announcement.
The “private health cameos” document, obtained through a freedom of information request from the Coalition, forecast the policy’s impact on fictional characters before Health Minister Mark Butler adopted it.
In one case, a Geelong-based retiree in her late 70s with an income of about $30,000 would drop private health insurance.
The retiree – dubbed Heather – needed a hip replacement and decided to rely on the public health system.
“Heather realises that, in addition to struggling with the additional cost of her premium, she cannot afford the out-of-pocket costs of having her hip replacement in the private system,” says the document by the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing.
In another fictional case study produced by the department, a Launceston couple on a $47,000 pension chose to re-evaluate gold health cover that they had held for most of their lives.
The couple, “Barbara and Joe”, were slugged an extra $298 under the policy and had to make budget sacrifices to keep their insurance. “In order to pay for the increased private health insurance, on top of increasing cost of living, they have to cut back with other expenses,” the document says.
The document also says the “department has not consulted on the specific proposed changes to the rebate due to the sensitivities involved”.
Opposition health spokeswoman Anne Ruston said the document showed government officials “wrote out in black and white” that pensioners would be seriously impacted under the policy. “When Mark Butler’s own department is writing scenarios that show pensioners will be forced to give up or go without, that’s not a fringe scenario, it’s the government’s own evidence of this policy in action,” Senator Ruston said.
NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said scenarios outlined by the federal department were concerning and would increase pressure on public hospitals.
“The public health system in NSW is already under a lot of pressure, with older people stranded in our hospitals and unable to leave because they cannot access a commonwealth government aged-care place,” Mr Park said. “That’s not fair on them and they deserve better. These new projections are very concerning and show the commonwealth government is just adding to this pressure by sending even more people into our public hospitals.” Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls said the “entirely unforeseen” policy decision by the Albanese government would increase demand for public healthcare and was not raised during negotiations on the recent hospital funding deal.
“To add insult to injury, during the negotiations, the Prime Minister asked states to ‘reduce growth in hospital activity’ to reduce costs,” Mr Nicholls said.
“In a system where 80 per cent of hospital activity is unplanned care in the emergency department, the Prime Minister wants us to shut the doors and yet he is giving older Australians nowhere else to go.” Tasmanian Health Minister Bridget Archer said she had written to Mr Butler asking him to reconsider the “deeply concerning” policy. She said it was “yet another cost-shift from the commonwealth to the states”.
“Tasmania has the fastest-ageing population in the country, and any increase in premiums will mean many older Tasmanians will be forced to downgrade or leave private health insurance altogether, forcing them into the Tasmanian public health system,” she said. “This will drive increased demand and longer hospital stays, and escalate pressures on public hospitals, particularly in emergency departments and elective surgery waitlists.” The government’s policy change, projected to raise $3bn over four years, would remove higher rebates for over 65s, which were introduced by the Howard government. Under the existing system, families on the basic tier earning less than $202,000 a year (or singles earning less than $101,000) will receive a 24 per cent rebate if they are aged under 65, 28 per cent if they are aged 65-69 and 32 per cent for those over 70. In tier two, singles earning $118-000-$158,000 or families on $236,000-$316,000 receive an 8 per cent rebate, rising to 12 per cent for 65 to 69-year-olds and 16 per cent for those over 70. Those earning more receive no rebate.
Mr Butler said giving different support based on age was “not fair between generations” and “not the best way to spend precious taxpayers’ dollars on behalf of older Australians when we need to do so much heavy lifting in aged care”. “Older Australians will still receive a rebate – of between 8 per cent to 24 per cent depending on income – the same as everyone else,” he said.
Mr Butler said all revenue raised from the reform would be redirected into the aged-care system, including 5000 more beds a year and a change to the Support at Home program to ensure personal services such as assisted showering are covered.
He said the Health Department predicted a “very small” number of people – 44,000 or 0.4 per cent of the insured population – would dump their coverage because of the policy change.
But a RedBridge poll commissioned by Private Healthcare Australia showed 15 per cent of over 65s would be “much more likely” and 24 per cent “somewhat more likely” to dump their coverage under the policy. The polling shows voters with a household income of less than $1000 a week would be the most likely to consider dropping insurance.
The poll of more than 1500 respondents also shows support for pensioners being exempt from the policy was 33 percentage points higher than opposition to it, while the margin was 44 points among Labor voters. But in a sign the political debate has a long way to go on the issue, 67 per cent of voters were unaware of the policy change until they were told about it by the pollsters.
Separate qualitative research by RedBridge showed the “intergenerational fairness” argument to justify the policy change “collapses on contact with voters of every age cohort tested”. “In the Gen Z group it does worse than collapse: it actively offends, in language of justice and division that is the most dangerous form of rejection a Labor government can attract from younger voters,” the RedBridge analysis says.
However, the quantitative polling did show support for the policy among 18 to 34-year-olds was 23 percentage points higher than opposition to it, while the margin among Labor voters was 14 percentage points.
Private Healthcare Australia chief executive Rachel David said the polling showed the government had significantly underestimated the number of people who would exit the private health insurance system.
HEALTH DEPARTMENT CAMEOS ON THE REBATE PLAN Heather In her late 70s, lives in Geelong, has silver hospital cover. Annual income $30,000. Needs hip replacement but has put it off because of cost.
Annual premium of $2333; rebate of $750. Pays $1583 gap. Reform option: Rebate reduces to $583; insurance cost gap now $1750 a year.
Potential impact: Heather can't afford out-of-pocket costs; drops her cover and relies on the public system.
Barbara and Joe In their 70s, live in Launceston. Annual income $47,000. Comprehensive gold cover. Relative good health.
Annual premium of $3706; rebate of $1192; pay $2514 gap.
Reform option: Rebate reduced to $894; insurance cost gap now $2812. Potential impact: Barbara and Joe continue to pay for insurance but cut back on expenses.
